extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and creative writers interested in aesthetics and the philosophy of taste
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for judging works of imagination (taste, beauty, and the sublime), explaining what faculties (imagination, sensibility, judgment) operate, what qualities affect pleasure, and how novelty, pain/pleasure, and knowledge shape critical taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between wit (resemblance) and judgment (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit is chiefly conversant in tracing resemblances; the business of judgment is rather in finding differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use resemblance to produce vivid images that please the imagination (wit), but rely on judgment to detect differences and achieve critical exactness. A perfect union of wit and judgment is rare; overreliance on resemblance can produce pleasing but inaccurate effects (examples: Homer/oriental writers strike admirable similitudes but seldom exact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure from resemblance vs. satisfaction from judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind has a far greater alacrity and satisfaction in tracing resemblances than in searching for differences: by making resemblances we produce new images, we unite and enlarge our stock; but in making distinctions we offer no food to the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing for immediate imaginative pleasure, emphasize striking resemblances and metaphors; when aiming for critical approval or accuracy, cultivate distinction and precise differences. Be aware that general resemblance pleases novices who lack detailed knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste depends on knowledge and experience, not a separate faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical taste does not depend upon a superior principle in men, but upon superior knowledge; it is improved by experience and observation, and not by any natural faculty alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop taste by increasing domain knowledge (e.g., in art, anatomy, manners). Examples: a shoemaker notices shoe mistakes a painter misses; an anatomist spots muscular inaccuracies the painter overlooked. Lack of domain knowledge explains many apparent differences of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensibility and judgment jointly constitute good taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is partly made up of a perception of the primary pleasures of sense, of the secondary pleasures of the imagination, and of the conclusions of the reasoning faculty concerning their relations and human passions, manners, and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate both sensibility (to feel pleasure) and judgement (to reason about decorum, congruity, manners). Sensibility alone can make one easily affected but a poor critic; judgement alone without sensibility may be dry. Good taste requires both, trained by attention and exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree-based qualities require refined measures and attention
rubrics_metrics.description: When men come to settle which of two things has the advantage in qualities judged by degree (e.g., polish, smoothness, shades of colour), disagreement arises because there is no common measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For qualities judged by degree rather than by kind, rely on trained perception, expert standards, or common measures where possible (artisans/experts decide subtle gradations). Accept that small differences are hard to adjudicate without specialized knowledge or tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works concerning manners, characters, and actions fall under judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Works extending to manners, characters, actions, relations, virtues, and vices come within the province of the judgment, which is improved by attention and the habit of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or evaluating fiction and drama, pay careful attention to plausibility, consistency of character, observance of time and place, and decency. These are learnable skills often taught by philosophy and experience; they constitute refined critical taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of wrong taste: defects of judgment rather than of sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A wrong taste arises from a defect of judgment caused by natural weakness of understanding or, more commonly, from want of proper and well-directed exercise; ignorance, inattention, prejudice, rashness, levity, and obstinacy pervert judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid intellectual vices (prejudice, rashness). Improve judgment through disciplined study, attention, and habitual reasoning. Recognize that quick, presumptive decisions about taste often reflect rashness, not superior insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (curiosity) as a necessary ingredient
rubrics_metrics.description: Curiosity (the desire for or pleasure in novelty) is the first and simplest emotion; some degree of novelty must be one of the materials in every instrument which works upon the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce some novelty to engage readers, especially adults whose curiosity is less easily satisfied. Pure novelty is superficial and fleeting—combine it with other powers (passions, imagination) to produce lasting effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects must be capable of exciting pain or pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: To move the passions of people advanced in life to any considerable degree, objects must, besides being somewhat new, be capable of exciting pain or pleasure from other causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting emotional impact, ensure material can evoke clearly positive or negative sensations. Relying solely on novelty will not sustain engagement; use morally or sensually charged content to arouse stable emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain and pleasure are positive and distinct (not just relative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pain and pleasure are simple ideas of a positive nature; they are not necessarily dependent on the removal or diminution of one another for their existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In writing and criticism, treat pleasure and pain as independent affective states. Do not assume that relieving pain always produces the same feeling as positive pleasure; their phenomenology differs and should be represented distinctively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'delight' (relative pleasure) from positive pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling that results from the ceasing or diminution of pain is not sufficiently like positive pleasure to be considered of the same nature; such relative pleasure is usefully termed 'delight'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distinct terms and craft distinct effects when depicting the relief of pain/danger versus the presence of positive joy. Relief-from-danger produces awe-tinged sobriety or tranquillity, not the same buoyant feeling as positive pleasure—represent these differences in tone and gesture.
